We thank the reviewer for their careful read of our submission and the helpful feedback.

Weaknesses:
> Although Section 3.1 offers interesting theoretical results, these results rely primarily on randomness and i.i.d. assumptions. It is currently unclear to what extent they can be generalized to real-world settings. In addition, I find that Section 3.1 is almost independent of the rest of the paper.

Thank you for the comment. We would like to clarify that we only make an i.i.d. assumption for the initialization of the weights, which is a standard assumption. The results in sec. 3 should be understood as for any confidence level, we can choose a width so that we obtain the desired property. We do not believe that this is an overly restrictive assumption.
The transformations to the feature representations resemble a rewiring of the geometric graph approximating the manifold that resembles a discrete Ricci flow. Our theoretical results show that such a rewiring is possible in nonlinear networks, but not in linear ones. This shows that nonlinearities are crucial in enabling the Ricci flow-like feature evolution that we study empirically in the subsequent sections.

> Lines 353–354 state: “these findings provide compelling evidence that the evolution of feature geometry in deep neural networks is fundamentally curvature-driven, closely aligned with Ricci flow.” In my view, the authors appear to conflate correlation with causation. Table 1 only shows a negative correlation between  and ; it does not establish that the former causes the latter. 

We thank the reviewer for the comment. We merely state that our empirical observations provide evidence that the evolution of feature geometry resembles a discrete Ricci flow. A formal proof that would establish a causal link is beyond the scope of this work. 

> The gradual shrinkage of distances among similar samples across layers is likely driven by their sharing the same labels, rather than by mean curvature.

This intuition that distances among similar samples shrinks across layers is actually in line with our observations. Similar samples belong to the same community, which corresponds to a positively curved region in the geometric graph (and also the underlying data manifold that it approximates). Positively curved regions contract under the Ricci flow. Please see Section 4.2 for a more detailed discussion.

> This paper is empirical. While it reports several interesting phenomena, it remains unclear how these findings could benefit the deep-learning community. Could the authors articulate potential application scenarios for these findings? Doing so would substantially strengthen the paper.

Thank you for your suggestion. We would like to point out the potential applications of our empirical findings suggested in Section 4.3 and 4.4, including model design choices and geometrically informed training protocols.

Questions:
> Could you elaborate on the assumption used in Theorem 3.1 (line 229)? It seems to impose a kind of smoothness in the feature space. How do you justify that this assumption is appropriate?

Thank you for your question. The assumption in Theorem 3.1 is met as long as the k-th closest and the k+1-st closest neighbor of a point do not have the exact same distance from it. Since the sphere centered at the considered point (on which the k-th neighbor lies) has Borel measure zero in \R^n, we believe this assumption is not too restrictive.

> Given the material presented, considering node-level curvature appears more natural than edge-level curvature (e.g., node resistance curvature, combinatorial curvature, or diffusion curvature). Could the authors discuss this further?

Node-level curvature notions, such as resistance, combinatorial, or diffusion curvature, are indeed interesting and may provide valuable local insights. However, these metrics generally lack established continuum limits that connect graph curvature to manifold curvature in the same way as Ollivier-Ricci curvature. Exploring node-level curvature in this context is an interesting direction for future work. We have added a note on this in the future work section.

> Based on the results in Figure 5, as the number of layers increases further, is it possible for the Layer-Ricci coefficient to become positive?

Yes, as the number of layers increases, it is possible for the Layer-Ricci coefficient to become positive.

summary.value: This paper studies how data representations change across layers of neural networks. It builds k-nearest-neighbor graphs on the samples at each layer and measures how their pairwise distances and discrete Ricci curvature evolve. Across many of trained feed-forward ReLU networks, the authors find that regions of positive curvature contract and negative curvature expand, mirroring the behavior of Ricci flow in geometry. Thus, network depth acts like a discrete time variable of a geometric flow on the data manifold. Experiments on synthetic, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 binary tasks confirm this trend. The study attempts to highlight that deep learning implicitly performs a curvature-driven transformation of the data manifold. It also suggests geometric heuristics for early stopping and optimal depth based on when curvature evolution saturates.

Thank you for these insightful questions. The result should be understood as follows: for any desired confidence level (probability), sample size, and epsilon, we can choose the width large enough (with an explicit bound) so that the desired property holds. However, in practice, we observed that the required width to achieve isometry is often much smaller than the bound stated in Theorem 3.1—this is expected, since the proof employs Boole’s inequality, which typically leads to a loose upper bound.

> A few more questions: Is the lower bound independent for all ? That is a bit counter intuitive to me. Is  (the size of the neighborhood) something you choose?

It is indeed surprising that the result is independent of the neighborhood size; however, we remark that epsilon depends on k. Specifically, epsilon measures the difference between the distance to the k-th closest neighbor and the k+1-st closest neighbor—the larger this gap, the smaller the necessary width for the bound to hold. Consequently, the dependency of epsilon on k is not, for instance, monotonic.

> Also, I realize that assuming data sampled from within a unit ball is common practice but your work hints at an underlying geometric structure of data and I wonder how that is captured in the toy setting in A.4.1.

Although later sections of our work rely on geometric structure in the data, this initial theoretical result is independent of such structure and remains valid even when no inherent geometry is present, as in the toy setting of Appendix A.4.1.

Overall, I enjoyed reading this paper (although I am not an expert in Ricci curvature or neural network feature geometry).

I have two main reservations for this paper. The first is that the paper is overstating the significance of its results. The introduction states "We propose a novel early-stopping heuristic that leverages the emergence of curvature-driven geometric behavior during training (Sec. 4.3).4. By analyzing layer-wise curvature-driven transformations, we introduce a geometric criterion for network depth selection (Sec. 4.4)." In my opinion, this is overstated. The authors show some empirical evidence that the behavior of the Layer-Ricci coefficients might be correlated to the test accuracy. But this evidence is circumstantial at best here, and while the authors could hypothesize that this could be used for layer selection or early stopping heuristic, they haven't tried it out. What would this bring compared to regular stopping criteria? While I appreciate the paper and the work that the authors have put in, I do think that the significance of the findings is a little overstated.


The second pertains the specifics of the experiments and conclusions of the authors (see questions below). In particular, the authors don't spend too much time discussing the choice of the number of neighbors k. One could argue that Figure 14 shows some signs of sensitivity to $k$ (also, it might be worthwhile to add error bars on these plots). Did you use symmetric‑kNN (edge if either is in the other’s kNN) or mutual‑kNN? How sensitive are results to this choice and to feature normalization between layers?

questions.value:
1) What distance is the local change of distances based on? I'm assuming Euclidean? Can you also explain why it makes sense to compare layer to layer using a Euclidean distance? I would have thought that Euclidean distances would not be the best to compare from layer to layer. So agreed, the correlation takes care of scaling --- but what if you used a spearman instead? Would that be more robust?

2) I am not sure I understand the point of the community structure experiment: "While removing such a small fraction of samples should not noticeably alter the graph geometry, it leads to a qualitatively different behavior: the curvature gap increases consistently across layers instead of collapsing." Doesn't this mean that the metric that the authors are using is extremely sensitive to just a few outliers (5 misclassified points out of 1,000)? Wouldn't this be a red flag for using this method to diagnose problems/ early stopping, etc?

Thank you for raising these points. Ideally, we would use the geodesic distance on the underlying manifold, but since the data manifold is unobservable, we do not have access to the geodesic distances. Instead, we rely on the shortest path distance within the k-NN graph as a discrete analogue of the shortest path distance on the manifold. We have added a clarifying note in the revised manuscript. We have also included additional results using Spearman correlation in Table 10 in the revised manuscript to further assess robustness. The results align closely with those obtained using the Pearson correlation.

> I am not sure I understand the point of the community structure experiment: "While removing such a small fraction of samples should not noticeably alter the graph geometry, it leads to a qualitatively different behavior: the curvature gap increases consistently across layers instead of collapsing." Doesn't this mean that the metric that the authors are using is extremely sensitive to just a few outliers (5 misclassified points out of 1,000)? Wouldn't this be a red flag for using this method to diagnose problems/ early stopping, etc?

Thank you for raising this concern. As discussed in Section 4.2, we dismiss the curvature gap as a useful measure for community structure due to its sensitivity to outliers, and instead rely on classical metrics such as modularity and normalized cut. Furthermore, we emphasize that the results in the later sections—including the early stopping heuristic—do not depend on the curvature gap but are instead based on our local Ricci evolution coefficients, which are based on discrete Ricci flow, rather than the curvature gap.

summary.value:
**Summary:**
This paper explores the evolution of neural feature geometry in neural networks through the lens of discrete geometry. The authors undertake a phenomenological study where they construct a knn graph and study the evolution of the graph through the network. Armed with this construction, they introduce the concept of a local Ricci evolution coefficient and measure whether network-induced geometric transformations resemble discrete Ricci flows. They then take this framework to synthetic and real-world binary classification tasks which show negative coefficients, implying a learned curvature driven dynamics.

**Rationale:**
This paper is interesting and contributes a novel perspective, but has several significant issues which limit its contributions. The theoretical analysis is too idealized, the practical implications are suggestive but unvalidated, and the experimental scope is limited to small models. Further, the reviewers are roughly aligned that this paper is roughly borderline within clear champion. Taken together, the paper is sadly a borderline reject. Despite this, I'd recommend that the authors give this work just a little more time in the oven -- it's a beautiful perspective and would be a truly lovely contribution with a little more work.

summary.value: The paper studies how features of a neural network evolve as a function of the the depth over the training dynamics under the manifold hypothesis. They show that a linear neural network (NN) can only learn an isometric transformation with high probability. They then argue for the importance of non-linearity in learning meaningful feature representations. They then study the changes in feature geoemtry across layers using a *local Ricci evolution coefficient*. Their experiments show efficacy of this framework and also a new phenomena reflected in the curvature gap which relates to data filtering.

strengths.value: The paper is well written with an argument that the authors build up intuitively. I particularly liked the idea of discretizing a continuous curved space to measure the curvature. Their use of the Ollivier-Ricci curvature is apt and clever. The authors build up to Section 3.2 where they present local Ricci coefficient in an intuitive manner. The various graphs and figures (including in the Appendix) help back their theoretical argument. Their measure correlates well with various phenomena such as over-fitting and data filtering.

comment.value:
Questions:
> Line 173:" While this definition is well-founded in Forman’s framework and computationally efficient, it is often too simplistic to capture the geometric complexity required in many applications": why is it too simplistic?

Thank you for your question. For example, a key limitation of the Forman-Ricci curvature is that it disregards the number of triangles adjacent to an edge, one of the most elementary and important geometric properties of a graph (see Jost & Liu, 2014). This simplification means that important local geometric features, such as clustering and community structure that are reflected in triangle counts, are not captured by Forman-Ricci curvature. Since a characterization of those features is crucial for our analysis, the classical (unaugmented) Forman-Ricci curvature is too simplistic for our analysis. To further support this point, we calculated the local Ricci evolution coefficients using the classical Forman-Ricci curvature, as shown in Table 9. As anticipated, the correlation observed in previous experiments is substantially reduced or absent when using the unaugmented curvature, validating the necessity of a more expressive measure for our purposes

> Line 234: what is the meaning of ? Does it mean isomorphism? I would introduce the symbol in text before the theorem. If this was explained in the paper and I missed it please let me know.

Thank you for pointing this out. You are correct; the symbol denotes that the two graphs are isomorphic. We have introduced and clarified this notation in the revised version of the manuscript. 

> Figure 1: What neural network architecture are you using here?

Figure 1 is a schematic Figure intended to illustrate the underlying idea and is not based on any specific neural network architecture. 

> figure 5: width is fixed at 25: can you remark how this would change for larger widths? I would expect the the Layer-Ricci coeeficient to vary across widths or maybe stabilize at larger widths.

This is a very good question. We ran the same experiments for varying widths between 25 and up to 100 hidden neurons, and consistently observed that the Layer-Ricci coefficients followed the same trends across different depths. However, for larger widths, the coefficients started to increase again at earlier layers. 

> Question related to Ansuini et al. 2017: If the intrinsic dimensionality of feature representations is changing across layers (Figure 3 by Ansuini et al) then how do you relate it to your result on Layer-Ricci coefficients? I see that your measure is over discrete graphs but I assume the edge density of the graphs changes as intrinsic data dimensionality changes.

Thank you for this very interesting question. Since we construct k-nearest neighbor graphs at each layer, the edge density is largely determined by k and does not significantly change as the intrinsic dimensionality varies. However, we did not investigate the relationship between changes in intrinsic dimensionality and the behavior of Layer-Ricci coefficients. This is a very interesting question that merits a detailed empirical investigation, which is unfortunately beyond the scope of the current paper. We have added a note in the future directions regarding this excellent point.

> Line 708: "depth increases representational power" In randomly initialized neural networks Hanin et al [1] found that depth doesn't necessarily increase representational power beyond the number of neurons. Moreover, Brahma et al show that depth helps disentangle the manifolds. I am not sure if this statement can be made with high accuracy as of now.

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the relationship between depth and representational power in neural networks is nuanced and context-dependent. Our intention was to refer to the result from Pascanu et al. (2013) and Montúfar et al. (2014), which showed that deep ReLU networks can represent exponentially more linear regions than shallow networks with the same number of units. We have now clarified this in the revised main text.

summary.value: The paper analogizes the evolution of features in neural networks to a discrete Ricci flow and, on this basis, provides several interesting proofs and empirical findings.

strengths.value: The paper offers an interesting new perspective on understanding how features evolve in neural networks and provides some mathematical justification based on random matrix theory. The experimental results—especially Section 4.4—are interesting and reveal how features evolve as the number of layers increases.

weaknesses.value:
* Although Section 3.1 offers interesting theoretical results, these results rely primarily on randomness and i.i.d. assumptions. It is currently unclear to what extent they can be generalized to real-world settings. In addition, I find that Section 3.1 is almost independent of the rest of the paper.

* Lines 353–354 state: “these findings provide compelling evidence that the evolution of feature geometry in deep neural networks is fundamentally curvature-driven, closely aligned with Ricci flow.” In my view, the authors appear to conflate correlation with causation. Table 1 only shows a negative correlation between $\mathcal O(x)$ and $\eta(x)$; it does not establish that the former causes the latter. The gradual shrinkage of distances among similar samples across layers is likely driven by their sharing the same labels, rather than by mean curvature.

* This paper is empirical. While it reports several interesting phenomena, it remains unclear how these findings could benefit the deep-learning community. Could the authors articulate potential application scenarios for these findings? Doing so would substantially strengthen the paper.

We would like to emphasize that our paper introduces a novel methodological framework for studying learned feature transformations, which we study empirically in detail for feedforward networks. > k-NN graphs may poorly capture manifold geometry in high dimensions.

Thank you for the comment. We acknowledge that the ability of k-NN graphs to approximate manifold geometry depends on sample size, the choice of k, the (unobservable) data distribution, and the sample density. However, the construction of discrete manifold approximation in this manner is standard in geometric data analysis. Importantly, in the ideal case of dense sampling, consistency results between the Ollivier-Ricci graph curvature and the Ricci curvature of the underlying manifold exist, which provides theoretical grounding for our proposed method [1].

Thank you for this suggestion. Exploring Ricci flow metrics for standard kernel-based feature extraction methods is indeed an interesting direction. However, this falls beyond the current scope of our work, which is focused on neural feature representations. We have added this as a future direction in the discussion section.
